newsitem.title: USA: Technique could stop unneeded appendectomies in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Technique could stop unneeded appendectomies in U.S.

text.p: A new diagnostic technique could prevent unnecessary appendectomies, 50,000 of which are performed yearly in the United States alone, a researcher said Tuesday.

"With our technique, an accurate diagnosis was made before surgery in 98 percent of all cases, and 100 percent of all cases of true appendicitis were accurately identified," said Patrick Rao of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston.
In the new technique, called focused appendix CT (FACT), a dye inserted in the lower right abdomen is scanned by computed tomography, which is available in most large U.S. hospitals.

The cost of the technique is $230, about half that of a conventional computer tomography exam and a fraction of the average $4,700 cost for surgeries performed each year for suspected appendicitis, about a quarter million of which are performed in the United States each year.
Rao, in a report at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, said one in five of the surgeries is later found to be unnecessary.
Standard X-rays diagnose correctly only 10 percent of cases, he added.
In a study of 100 patients who underwent FACT, 59 patients were diagnosed with appendicitis, of which only two turned out to have been an inaccurate diagnosis.

An alternative diagnosis was made in 33 of 41 patients who were determined not to have appendicitis. The most common alternative illness was mesenteric adentis, an inflation of the lymph nodes caused by an infection in the bowel that seldom required treatment, Rao said.
